Predictions for flexCountReg models

Source: R/predict_flexCountReg.R
predict.flexCountReg.Rd

Generates predictions for the expected count (lambda) for observations.

For countreg_rp (Random Parameters) models, three methods are available:

  • Simulated: Uses Halton draws to simulate the random parameters and averages the outcomes. This is a simulation-based approximation.

  • Individual (alias EB): Empirical Bayes observation-specific predictions (Wood and Gayah, 2025, Eqs. 5-7). Each simulation draw is weighted by the likelihood of the unit's observed outcomes (all of a panel's rows when panel_id was used), giving conditional coefficients \(E[\beta_i | y_i]\). By default these are used in the mean function, as in the paper; pass eb_type = "mean" to instead return the conditional mean \(E[\mu_{it} | y_i]\). The conditional coefficients and their conditional standard deviations are returned as the attributes "eb_coefficients" and "eb_sd". Requires the outcome (and the panel_id column, if used) in newdata, so it is meant for data with observed outcomes.

  • Exact: Uses the moment generating functions (MGFs) of the random parameter distributions (Wood and Gayah, 2025, Appendix A), including heterogeneity in means and variances. This is exact for normal, uniform, triangular and gamma parameters and has no simulation error. For lognormal parameters with \(x < 0\) the lognormal MGF has no closed form, and the Laplace approximation of Asmussen, Jensen and Rojas-Nandayapa (2016) is used: accurate, but approximate despite the method's name (it needs the lamW package). For \(x > 0\) with a lognormal parameter (and for gamma parameters with \(x\sigma^2/\mu \ge 1\)) the expected value is infinite, and Inf is returned with a warning, for both Exact and Simulated predictions. Whether the expected value exists is decided from the parameters alone, so Simulated predictions do not need lamW. A finite expected value too large to represent is reported as an overflow.

For countreg, poisLindRE, and RENB models, the function calculates the expected value \(\mu = \exp(X\beta)\) (with appropriate adjustments for specific families like PLN, PLL or underreporting).

Usage

# S3 method for class 'flexCountReg'
predict(
  object,
  newdata = NULL,
  ...,
  type = c("response", "true", "prob_reported", "link", "prob", "zero"),
  new_data = NULL,
  interval = c("none", "confidence", "prediction"),
  level = 0.95
)

Arguments

object

a model object estimated using this R package.

newdata

optional data frame for which to generate predictions. It must contain every variable used by the model's formulas (including rpar_formula, dis_param_formula_1/2, underreport_formula and heterogeneity formulas) and any offset columns. The outcome is not required. If omitted, predictions are made for the data used to fit the model.

...

optional arguments passed to the function. This includes method. Passing the data as data = is deprecated; use newdata.

type

the type of prediction. "response" (default) is the expected observed count. For models with underreporting this is \(\mu \times p\), the true mean times the probability of being reported. "true" is the true expected count \(\mu\) (excluding the underreporting probability), "prob_reported" is the probability of being reported \(p\), and "link" is the linear predictor \(X\beta\) plus the offset. For models without underreporting, "true" equals "response" and "prob_reported" is 1. For zero-inflated and hurdle models (zero_formula), "response" includes the zero model, "true" is the mean of the count distribution alone, and "zero" is the probability from the zero model: the probability of a structural zero (zero-inflated) or of a zero count (hurdle). "prob" returns a matrix of probabilities \(P(Y = k)\) with one row per row of newdata and one column per count, for rootograms and for scoring models out of sample (see the section Count probabilities). It is available for every estimator; the other types besides "response" for countreg models only.

new_data

the same as newdata, under the name used by tidymodels. Give one or the other.

interval

"none" (default), "confidence" or "prediction". See the section Intervals.

level

the confidence or prediction level of the interval.

Value

A numeric vector of predicted expected counts for each observation in the provided data. If no data is provided, the predictions for the data used in estimating the model are provided. With interval = "confidence" or "prediction", a data frame with columns fit, lwr and upr (see the section Intervals).

Details

The returned vector always has one element per row of newdata, in the same order. Rows with missing values in any variable the estimate needs get NA: a row with a missing distribution-parameter, zero-model or reporting covariate has no count distribution, so its probabilities (type = "prob") and intervals are NA, while its expected count is returned when it does not depend on that parameter (for example the NB2 mean) and is NA otherwise. Factor levels and contrasts from the training data are used, so newdata may contain only a subset of the levels. An error is raised if an offset column is missing from newdata.

Note

optional parameter method: Only valid for random parameters models (countreg_rp). Options include Simulated (default), Individual (or EB), or Exact.

optional parameter eb_type: for method = "Individual", either "coefficients" (default) or "mean".

Count probabilities

For type = "prob", these arguments (in ...) choose the counts:

  • counts: the counts, non-negative whole numbers such as 0:10, 5:8 or c(0, 1, 10). Only these are evaluated, so a range far from zero is as cheap as one near it.

  • max_count: short for counts = 0:max_count; the default is the largest count in the training data.

  • overflow = TRUE: add a last column ">k" with the probability of a count above the largest one.

  • underflow = TRUE: add a first column "<k" with the probability of a count below the smallest one. With both, the rows of a contiguous range sum to 1.

The probabilities are those of the marginal distribution of one count of a new unit: the unit's random terms are integrated out in closed form (renb, repois, poislind_re, negmultinom) or by Gauss-Hermite quadrature or scrambled Halton draws (countreg_rp). For negmultinom models of type NM1 and NM-P the frailty depends on the total mean of the cluster, taken over the cluster's rows in newdata (every row is its own cluster without the grouping columns). countreg_fe models use the estimated group effects. Finite mixtures, hierarchical, multivariate and allocation models: predict.countreg_mix, predict.countreg_hier, predict.countreg_mv, predict.countreg_alloc.

Intervals of other estimators

The estimators other than countreg() use draws from the asymptotic normal distribution of the estimates: ndraws scrambled Halton points (default 500 for confidence and 200 for prediction intervals), with seed. Parameters without a usable standard error (none, or the log of a distribution parameter with one above 10, which is at a boundary) are held at their estimates, with a message. Prediction intervals are the quantiles of the predictive distribution, the count probabilities averaged over the draws (up to max_count, default 1e4), and are for one count of a new unit, including its random terms. countreg_fe models have none: their group effects have no covariance matrix. The parametric bootstrap (uncertainty = "bootstrap") is for countreg models.

Intervals

For countreg models, interval = "confidence" gives a confidence interval for the expected count (type = "response", the expected observed count, or "true"), and interval = "prediction" a prediction interval for one future observed count (type = "response"). The result is then a data frame with columns fit, lwr and upr, with the settings in the attribute "interval". For content tolerance intervals see tolerance_interval.

Estimation uncertainty is represented by parameter vectors chosen by the optional argument uncertainty (in ...):

  • "normal" (default): the asymptotic normal distribution of the estimates, \(\hat\theta + R^\top z\) with \(R^\top R\) the covariance matrix and \(z\) the standard normal quantiles of ndraws (default 500) Halton points. Halton sequences are deterministic, so the intervals are reproducible and have less simulation error than pseudo-random draws; for models with many parameters, scrambled = TRUE (with a seed) uses scrambled Halton points, which avoid the correlation between high dimensions of the standard sequence. When the covariance matrix is not positive definite (e.g. a dispersion parameter at its boundary) the parametric bootstrap is used instead, with a message.

  • "bootstrap": a parametric bootstrap. bootstraps (default 200) response vectors are simulated from the fitted model on the training rows and the model is refit to each with its frozen specification; refits that fail or do not converge are rejected and counted. Use seed for reproducibility. Not available for models with weights.

The confidence interval takes the \((1 - level)/2\) and \((1 + level)/2\) quantiles of the expected count over these parameter vectors. The prediction interval uses the predictive distribution of the count, the probability mass function of the observed count averaged over the parameter vectors, and returns its integer quantiles: the smallest counts \(L\) and \(U\) with \(P(Y \le L) \ge (1 - level)/2\) and \(P(Y \le U) \ge (1 + level)/2\). Because counts are discrete, the predictive coverage is usually above level; the limits are not interpolated. Both include zero-inflated, hurdle and underreporting components. max_count (in ..., default 1e5) bounds the counts used to resolve the upper tail.

In a Monte Carlo study of Poisson and NB2 regressions (n = 30 and 200), prediction intervals at level 0.90 covered 0.93 to 0.97 of future counts, while plug-in intervals that ignore estimation uncertainty fell to 0.88 for the smaller sample.

References

Wood, J.S., Gayah, V. (2025). Out-of-sample prediction and interpretation for random parameter generalized linear models. Accident Analysis and Prevention, 220, 108147.

Examples

# \donttest{
# Load data and create a dummy variable
data("washington_roads")
washington_roads$AADT10kplus <- ifelse(washington_roads$AADT > 10000, 1, 0)

# =========================================================================
# 1. Fixed Parameter Model (countreg)
# =========================================================================
nb2_fixed <- countreg(Total_crashes ~ lnaadt + lnlength + speed50,
                      data = washington_roads, 
                      family = "NB2")
pred_fixed <- predict(nb2_fixed, newdata = washington_roads)

# =========================================================================
# 2. Random Parameters Model (countreg_rp)
# =========================================================================
rp_nb2 <- countreg_rp(Total_crashes ~ lnaadt + lnlength,
                      rpar_formula = ~ -1 + speed50,
                      data = washington_roads,
                      family = "NB2",
                      rpardists = c(speed50 = "n"),
                      ndraws = 100)

# Method A: Simulated (Default)
pred_sim <- predict(rp_nb2, newdata = washington_roads, method = "Simulated")

# Method B: Exact (Analytical MGF)
pred_exact <- predict(rp_nb2, newdata = washington_roads, method = "Exact")

# Method C: Individual (Empirical Bayes, requires the observed outcome)
pred_eb <- predict(rp_nb2, newdata = washington_roads, method = "Individual")

# =========================================================================
# 3. Random Effects Models (poisLindRE / RENB)
# =========================================================================
pl_re <- poisLind.re(Total_crashes ~ lnaadt + lnlength,
                     data = washington_roads,
                     group_var = "ID")
pred_pl_re <- predict(pl_re, newdata = washington_roads)
# }
